name: Rust
description: Ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, traits and fearless concurrency — the model that makes memory safety a compile-time property.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Rust is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is Rust, and what is it mainly used for?
cards.answer: A compiled systems language that offers C/C++-level performance with memory safety guaranteed at compile time — without a garbage collector. It is used for systems software, command-line tools, browsers, WebAssembly, embedded devices, cloud infrastructure and, increasingly, OS kernels (Linux, Windows).
cards.explanation: Most serious security bugs in C and C++ code are memory-safety bugs. Rust's compiler rejects programs that could have them, which is why governments and large companies now recommend memory-safe languages for new systems code.

cards.prompt: Where did Rust come from?
cards.answer: Graydon Hoare began it as a personal project in 2006; Mozilla sponsored it from 2009, and Rust 1.0 shipped in 2015. Since 2021 it has been stewarded by the independent Rust Foundation.
cards.explanation: Rust was used to build parts of Firefox (the Servo-derived CSS engine). It has topped Stack Overflow's "most admired language" survey for years, reflecting how much its users like it once past the learning curve.

cards.prompt: How is a Rust program built and run?
cards.answer: With Cargo: `cargo new hello` creates a project, `cargo run` compiles and runs it, `cargo build --release` produces an optimised native binary. Under the hood `rustc` compiles via LLVM to machine code.
cards.explanation: Rust compiles slower than Go because the compiler does a lot of checking and optimisation. The toolchain itself is installed and updated with `rustup`.

cards.prompt: What does a minimal Rust program look like?
cards.answer: `fn main()` is the entry point. `println!` is a macro (the `!` marks it), which lets it check the format string at compile time.
cards.explanation: Variables are immutable by default (`let x = 5;`); you opt into mutation with `let mut`. That default is a small example of Rust's general approach: make the safe choice the easy one.

cards.prompt: How does Rust manage memory without a garbage collector?
cards.answer: Through ownership: every value has exactly one owner, and it is freed automatically when the owner goes out of scope. Other code can borrow a value through references, and the borrow checker enforces at compile time that you have either many readers or one writer — never both.
cards.explanation: These rules eliminate use-after-free, double free and data races before the program ever runs. The cost is a learning curve: "fighting the borrow checker" is a real phase for every new Rust programmer.

resources.title: The Rust Book — What is ownership?

cards.prompt: Rust vs Go
cards.answer: Both are modern compiled languages popular for infrastructure. Go optimises for simplicity and fast development; Rust for control, safety and peak performance.

left.title: Rust
points: Rich type system, steep learning curve

right.title: Go
points: Network services, cloud and DevOps tools

cards.explanation: A common rule of thumb: Go for services and tooling a team needs to ship and maintain quickly; Rust where memory safety must coexist with C-level performance or no runtime at all.

modules.name: Ownership & Borrowing
modules.description: The core model: who owns a value, who may look at it, and for how long.

cards.prompt: State Rust's three ownership rules.
cards.answer: 1. Every value has exactly one owner. 2. There can be only one owner at a time. 3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.
cards.explanation: These rules give deterministic destruction without a garbage collector and without manual free. Everything else in Rust — moves, borrows, lifetimes — exists to let you work with values while keeping this invariant checkable at compile time.

resources.title: The Rust Book — What is ownership?

cards.prompt: What are the borrowing rules?
cards.answer: At any given time you may have either any number of shared references (`&T`) or exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`) — never both. References must never outlive the value they point to.
cards.explanation: Aliasing XOR mutation is the whole trick: data races, iterator invalidation and use-after-free all require aliasing plus mutation. Forbidding the combination eliminates the entire class at compile time, which is what 'fearless concurrency' actually means.

resources.title: The Rust Book — References and borrowing

cards.prompt: Why does this fail to compile, and why would it compile if `s` were an `i32`?
cards.answer: `String` owns a heap buffer, so `let t = s` **moves** it and `s` is no longer valid. `i32` implements `Copy`, so assignment duplicates the bits and the original stays usable.
cards.explanation: Types that own resources cannot be `Copy`. Use `s.clone()` for an explicit deep copy, or borrow with `&s` when the callee only needs to read. The compiler error names the moved value and the line that moved it.

resources.title: The Rust Book — Ownership and moves

cards.prompt: A lifetime annotation such as `'a` does not change how long a value lives — it ___ the relationship between the lifetimes of inputs and outputs.
cards.answer: describes
cards.explanation: Lifetimes are descriptive, not prescriptive. `fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str` tells the compiler the result may borrow from either input, so it can reject callers whose borrow would outlive the data. Elision rules infer most of them for you.

cards.prompt: `RefCell<T>` vs `Mutex<T>`
cards.answer: Both move borrow checking to runtime; RefCell is single-threaded, Mutex is thread-safe.

left.title: RefCell<T>
points: Panics on a conflicting borrow at runtime

right.title: Mutex<T>
points: Real locking cost, and deadlock is possible

cards.explanation: Rust's default is compile-time checking; these types opt into runtime checking when the ownership graph is genuinely dynamic. `Rc<RefCell<T>>` for single-threaded shared mutable state, `Arc<Mutex<T>>` across threads.

resources.title: The Rust Book — RefCell and interior mutability

modules.name: Types, Traits & Errors
modules.description: Enums, traits, generics and the error-handling model that replaced exceptions.

cards.prompt: How does Rust represent absence and failure, and why are there no exceptions?
cards.answer: `Option<T>` is `Some(T)` or `None`; `Result<T, E>` is `Ok(T)` or `Err(E)`. Both are ordinary enums, so the compiler forces you to handle every case — failure is in the type signature rather than hidden in the control flow.
cards.explanation: There is no null and no throw. `?` propagates an `Err` up one level with an automatic `From` conversion, which keeps error handling terse without hiding it. `panic!` exists for unrecoverable bugs, not for expected failure.

cards.prompt: What does the `?` operator expand to here?
cards.answer: On `Ok(v)` it evaluates to `v`; on `Err(e)` it returns early with `Err(From::from(e))` from the enclosing function.
cards.explanation: The `From` conversion is what lets `?` bubble different error types into one function-level error type — the basis of `anyhow::Error` in applications and `thiserror` enums in libraries.

resources.title: Rust reference — The question mark operator

cards.prompt: Rust traits vs Java/C# interfaces
cards.answer: Traits can be implemented for types you did not define, support default methods and associated types, and dispatch statically by default.

left.title: Rust trait
points: Implement for foreign types (subject to orphan rules)
Static dispatch via generics — monomorphised, inlinable

right.title: Interface
points: Must be declared on the type itself
Virtual dispatch by default (the JIT may devirtualise)

cards.explanation: `impl Trait` / generics compile to a specialised copy per concrete type — zero-cost but larger binaries. `dyn Trait` is one vtable-based copy, smaller and slower. Choose per call site, not per codebase.

cards.prompt: What do the `Send` and `Sync` marker traits mean?
cards.answer: `Send`: the type can be transferred to another thread. `Sync`: `&T` can be shared between threads (equivalently, `T: Sync` iff `&T: Send`). Both are auto-derived when all fields qualify.
cards.explanation: These two markers are how the compiler proves thread safety. `Rc<T>` is neither (non-atomic refcount); `Arc<T>` is both when `T: Send + Sync`. `Cell`/`RefCell` are `Send` but not `Sync`. Getting a data race past the compiler requires `unsafe`.

cards.prompt: How much work does this line do?
cards.answer: None. Iterator adaptors are lazy — nothing runs until a consuming adaptor such as `sum`, `collect`, `for` or `count` drives it.
cards.explanation: Because adaptors are generic structs resolved at compile time, the whole chain monomorphises and inlines into a single loop with no intermediate allocation — usually matching a hand-written loop exactly.

cards.prompt: What does `unsafe` actually permit, and what does it not?
cards.answer: It permits five things: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions or FFI, accessing mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits, and accessing union fields. It never disables the borrow checker or the type system.
cards.explanation: `unsafe` means 'I have checked the invariants the compiler cannot'. The idiom is to wrap a small unsafe core in a safe API and document the invariants. Verify with Miri, which detects UB in Rust code that ordinary tests miss.

cards.prompt: `String` vs `&str`
cards.answer: `String` is an owned, growable, heap-allocated UTF-8 buffer; `&str` is a borrowed view into UTF-8 bytes.

left.title: String
points: Return type when you produce new text

right.title: &str
points: A borrowed slice — pointer plus length
May point at a String, a literal, or static memory
The right parameter type for reading text

cards.explanation: Take `&str` in parameters and return `String` when producing owned data. Both are guaranteed valid UTF-8 — which is why indexing by byte position can panic on a char boundary, and why you iterate with `.chars()`.

modules.name: Enums, Patterns & Smart Pointers
modules.description: Algebraic data types, exhaustive matching, closures, trait objects, smart pointers and drop order.

cards.prompt: What makes Rust enums and `match` more powerful than enums in C or Java?
cards.answer: Each variant can carry its own data (`enum Shape { Circle { r: f64 }, Rect(f64, f64) }`) — a sum type — and `match` must be exhaustive, so the compiler rejects code that forgets a variant.
cards.explanation: This is how Rust models states and messages without nulls or invalid combinations: make illegal states unrepresentable. Adding a variant turns every non-exhaustive `match` into a compile error pointing at code to update. Avoid a catch-all `_` arm when you want that safety.

resources.title: The Rust Book — Enums and pattern matching

cards.prompt: When do you use `if let`, `let ... else` and `matches!` instead of a full `match`?
cards.answer: `if let Some(x) = opt { ... }` handles one pattern and ignores the rest. `let Some(x) = opt else { return Err(...) };` binds on success and forces the else branch to diverge — flattening early-return code. `matches!(v, Pattern)` returns a bool.
cards.explanation: `let ... else` keeps the happy path unindented, the same way guard clauses do in other languages. Use a full `match` when several arms carry meaningful logic, so exhaustiveness checking still protects you.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: `let x = x + 1` creates a *new* binding that shadows the old one — unlike `mut`, it can even change type. The inner block's shadow ends with the block, so the outer `x` is 6 again afterwards. `spaces` changing from `&str` to `usize` would be impossible with `mut`.

resources.title: The Rust Book — Variables and mutability — shadowing

cards.prompt: `Fn` vs `FnMut` vs `FnOnce`
cards.answer: The three closure traits describe how a closure uses its captures: `Fn` only reads them, `FnMut` mutates them, and `FnOnce` consumes (moves out of) them and can therefore be called only once.

right.title: FnOnce
points: Takes ownership of what it captured

cards.explanation: Every `Fn` is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`, so accept the loosest bound your function needs: `FnOnce` for a callback run once (`thread::spawn`, `Option::map`), `FnMut` for repeated calls that accumulate, `Fn` for shared concurrent use. `move` controls how captures are taken, not which trait is implemented.

cards.prompt: Generics (`impl Trait`) vs trait objects (`Box<dyn Trait>`)
cards.answer: Generics are resolved at compile time with a specialised copy per type; trait objects are resolved at runtime through a vtable, allowing different concrete types behind one pointer.

left.title: impl Trait / <T: Trait>
points: Monomorphised: one copy per concrete type
One concrete type per call site

right.title: Box<dyn Trait>
points: Mix different types in one collection
Heap allocation plus a fat pointer

cards.explanation: You need `dyn` for heterogeneous collections (`Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`) and to keep binary size down; generics when performance and inlining matter. A trait must be "dyn compatible" (object safe) — no generic methods or `Self`-returning methods — to be used as a trait object.

resources.title: The Rust Book — Using trait objects

cards.prompt: What are `Box<T>`, `Rc<T>` and `Arc<T>` for?
cards.answer: `Box<T>` is single-owner heap allocation — for recursive types, large values and trait objects. `Rc<T>` is shared ownership via a non-atomic reference count, single-threaded only. `Arc<T>` is the atomic, thread-safe equivalent.
cards.explanation: Rc and Arc give shared *immutable* access; add `RefCell` or `Mutex` for mutation. Reference cycles leak, just as in any refcounting scheme — break them with `Weak<T>`, typically for parent pointers in trees.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
end of main
drop b
drop a
cards.explanation: Values are dropped when their owner goes out of scope, in reverse order of declaration — like C++ destructors. Implementing `Drop` gives RAII: files close, locks release and guards restore state automatically. `std::mem::drop(x)` ends a value early; you cannot call `x.drop()` directly.

resources.title: The Rust Book — Running code on cleanup with the Drop trait

verify.expectedOutput:
end of main
drop b
drop a

cards.prompt: What does `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]` do, and when should you derive `Copy`?
cards.answer: It generates standard trait implementations from the fields: `Debug` for `{:?}` printing, `Clone` for explicit copies, `PartialEq`/`Eq` for `==`, `Hash` for use as a map key, plus `Default`, `PartialOrd`/`Ord` and others.
cards.explanation: Derive `Copy` only for small, plain values whose fields are all Copy (numbers, ids, small coordinate structs): it makes assignment an implicit bitwise copy. Once a type owns a heap resource it cannot be Copy, and adding Copy later is easy while removing it is a breaking change.

cards.prompt: What happens on integer overflow in Rust, and how do you choose the behaviour explicitly?
cards.answer: Debug builds panic; release builds wrap in two's complement (unless `overflow-checks` is enabled). Choose explicitly with `checked_add` (returns `Option`), `wrapping_add`, `saturating_add` or `overflowing_add`.
cards.explanation: Overflow is never undefined behaviour in Rust, unlike signed overflow in C. For values derived from untrusted input — sizes, lengths, offsets — use `checked_*` and handle `None`, or turn on overflow checks in release builds when correctness matters more than a little speed.

resources.title: The Rust Book — Data types — integer overflow

cards.prompt: `thiserror` vs `anyhow`
cards.answer: thiserror derives precise error enums for libraries; anyhow provides one easy dynamic error type with context for applications.

right.title: anyhow (applications)
points: Easy to report, hard to match on

cards.explanation: Libraries should expose typed errors so callers can match on them; binaries mostly want to add context and report. Both work with `?`. Reserve `unwrap()` for cases that truly cannot fail, and prefer `expect("why this cannot fail")` so a panic explains itself.

modules.name: Cargo, Async & Tooling
modules.description: Cargo and crates, modules and visibility, testing, clippy, async runtimes and editions.

cards.prompt: What does Cargo do, and what are `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock`?
cards.answer: Cargo is Rust's build system and package manager: it resolves and downloads crates from crates.io, compiles, runs tests (`cargo test`), benchmarks, docs and binaries. `Cargo.toml` declares metadata and dependency ranges; `Cargo.lock` pins exact versions.
cards.explanation: Commit `Cargo.lock` for applications (and, per current guidance, for libraries too, for reproducible CI). Workspaces share one lockfile and target directory across several crates. `cargo add`, `cargo tree` and `cargo update -p` cover everyday dependency work.

cards.prompt: How do modules and visibility work in Rust?
cards.answer: Everything is private to its module by default. `pub` exposes an item, `pub(crate)` exposes it within the crate only, and `pub(super)` to the parent module. Modules map to files (`mod net;` loads `net.rs` or `net/mod.rs`), and `use` brings paths into scope.
cards.explanation: Privacy is per module, not per type, so tests in a child `mod tests` can reach private functions. Keep the public surface small and re-export the intended API from the crate root with `pub use`, so internal layout can change without breaking users.

resources.title: The Rust Book — Managing growing projects with packages, crates, and modules

cards.prompt: Where do unit tests, integration tests and doc tests live in a Rust crate?
cards.answer: Unit tests sit beside the code in a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` with `#[test]` functions and can reach private items. Integration tests live in `tests/` and use only the public API. Doc tests are code examples in `///` comments, compiled and run by `cargo test`.
cards.explanation: Doc tests keep examples honest — a broken example fails the build, the same idea as verified flashcards. `#[should_panic]` tests expected panics, and tests can return `Result` to use `?`.

resources.title: The Rust Book — Writing automated tests

cards.prompt: Rust's official linter, run with `cargo ___`, catches hundreds of common mistakes and non-idiomatic patterns beyond what the compiler warns about.
cards.answer: clippy
cards.explanation: Run `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` in CI so style and lint regressions fail the build. Clippy lints are grouped (correctness, perf, style, pedantic); the defaults are sensible, and specific lints can be allowed per item with a justifying comment.

cards.prompt: How is async Rust different from async in JavaScript or C#?
cards.answer: A Rust future is inert: calling an `async fn` builds a state machine that does nothing until polled. There is no built-in runtime — you choose one (Tokio is the de facto standard) to drive futures, and `.await` yields control back to it.
cards.explanation: Futures compile to zero-allocation state machines, which is why async Rust is fast but has sharp edges: never block the executor with CPU work or blocking I/O (use `spawn_blocking`), and futures moved across threads must be `Send`. Dropping a future cancels it at its last `.await` point.

cards.prompt: What is a Rust edition, and why can crates on different editions work together?
cards.answer: An edition (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) is an opt-in set of language changes that would otherwise break code — new keywords, changed defaults. Each crate declares its own edition, and all editions compile to the same internal representation, so they link together freely.
cards.explanation: `cargo fix --edition` automates most migrations. This is how Rust evolves without a Python 2 → 3 style split: the ecosystem never has to move in lockstep.

cards.prompt: Complexity of `Vec::push`, `Vec::insert(0, x)`, `HashMap::get` and `BTreeMap::get`?
cards.answer: `push` amortised O(1); `insert(0, x)` O(n) because every element shifts; `HashMap::get` O(1) average; `BTreeMap::get` O(log n) with sorted iteration.

complexity.time: push O(1)*, insert(0) O(n), HashMap get O(1) avg, BTreeMap get O(log n)

cards.explanation: Use `VecDeque` when you push and pop at both ends. HashMap uses SipHash by default to resist hash-flooding attacks; swap in a faster hasher (FxHash, ahash) only for trusted keys in hot paths. BTreeMap is the choice when you need ordered iteration or range queries.
